guide:
Risk guide — judge the consequence of being wrong, not the subject matter.
Ask these two questions in order.

First: if this answer is wrong, can a person be harmed, or does it breach a
rule that exists to prevent harm — dosing and prescribing limits, sterile and
infection-control practice, consent and privacy rules, drug and device safety
rules, trial-safety reporting? If so it is critical,
at every stage. A dosing schedule, a sterilisation protocol and a discharge
instruction are critical while still in draft, because the draft is what gets
followed at the bedside and audited.

Not every published standard is one of those. A standard that exists for
quality, consistency or interoperability — broadcast loudness, file formats,
naming conventions, style guides — is not a harm rule, however formally it is
written and however much a breach embarrasses someone. Ask what the rule is
protecting, not whether a rule exists.

Second, if nobody can be harmed: has anything been committed to yet?
- high: the answer acts on a patient or a record — an order, a prescription, a
  dosing change, a result released to a chart — or is safety-critical in
  function even while still a draft, such as a dosing limit or an alarm
  threshold; or it ships as core system behaviour, a security boundary, or
  data integrity. A dose given stays given, and someone is in the room
- medium: the answer is still a decision, reversible until an order is placed
  or a protocol is approved — choosing between options, estimating a risk,
  summarising the evidence, setting a screening interval, taking a history
- low: presentation, copy, documentation or configuration that is trivially
  reversible and cannot hurt anyone

Work on something whose purpose is to protect — a backup, an interlock, an
alarm, a containment, a life-support system — is judged by what it protects,
not by the stage it is at. Planning the backup of a research data store is
planning work, and a wrong answer loses the study's records, so it is at least
high rather than medium. It is critical only if a person can be harmed: losing
data, samples or money, however much of it, is high.

A protocol, schedule, policy, setpoint band or limit that will be followed
repeatedly carries the consequence of everything it governs. Judge it by what
happens when it is followed, not by the fact that it is a document. A
sterilisation protocol, a return-to-play progression and a style guide are all
paperwork: if following it can harm someone or breach a regulated requirement
it is critical, and if the worst case is rework or an unhappy audience it stays
low or medium.

criteria.false: It asks what a guideline, a label, a regulation or another published document states.
criteria.true: It asks for a value that has to be computed, such as a dose, a rate, a score, a risk or a total.

needs_calculation.instructions: Look only at state["q0"]. Must the answer to this request be worked out by calculation from figures, and not read from a document?

criteria.false: It can be worked out from what the request itself states and general principles.
criteria.true: It turns on a figure or wording that a named or implied outside document holds.

needs_sources.instructions: Look only at state["q0"]. Can this request be answered correctly only with facts from an outside source, such as a guideline, a regulation, a label, a trial report or a published measurement?

criteria.false: The passage is about the subject but does not state what is asked, or is about something else.
criteria.true: The passage states the fact or figure the question asks for.

quote_answers.instructions: Look only at state["q0"]. Does the passage itself state an answer to the question it was quoted for?

criteria.false: They state a different fact, figure or verdict, or one contradicts the other.
criteria.true: They state the same fact, figure or verdict, even in other words or with more detail.

same_meaning.instructions: Look only at state["q0"]. Do the two values state the same thing for this ask?
